artifact.recommendation: Use staged canaries with automatic abort thresholds, backward-compatible additive schema changes, and a two-layer rollback policy: immediately disable the new routing path via feature flag when routing or error thresholds trigger, and automatically roll back the application for database read-pattern or persistent latency regressions. Start at 1% traffic for at least 12 minutes, then advance through progressively larger regional/global stages only after healthy observation windows, reaching 100% within one business day.
reasoning: This option limits initial exposure while testing behavior that cannot be reproduced perfectly in staging.
Automatic aborts are necessary because prior routing regressions became visible within four minutes, leaving little margin against the five-minute customer-error constraint.
A 1% canary needs approximately 12 minutes to provide useful latency evidence, so advancing earlier would weaken detection quality.
The additive schema permits application rollback without a schema downgrade, including rollback to the old version.

Feature-flag shutdown provides the fastest response to routing failures; the nine-minute application rollback should be reserved for database read-pattern changes or failures not neutralized by the flag.

A six-week wait for production-identical staging would materially delay the release without eliminating third-party latency uncertainty, while a global-at-once deployment creates unnecessary blast radius.
considerations: Define an automatic routing kill threshold that triggers before the customer error rate can remain above 1% for five minutes—for example, a short rolling-window threshold with a conservative buffer and immediate flag disablement.
Evaluate both global and per-region error rate and p95 latency so a regional regression is not hidden by aggregate metrics.
Keep each early stage live long enough to cover the 12-minute latency-signal requirement, with longer holds where traffic is sparse or regional variance is high.
Suggested progression is 1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, and 100%, subject to traffic-volume validation and a precomputed schedule that fits within one business day.
Freeze unrelated deployments, verify rollback artifacts before launch, assign an accountable operator, and retain manual stop authority even with automation.
Continue monitoring after 100% because the evidence establishes rapid detection for prior routing regressions, not every possible database or regional failure mode.
assumptions: Feature-flag propagation is fast and reliable enough to stop the new routing path within the five-minute error-budget window.
The old application version remains fully compatible with records containing the additive fields.
Sufficient observability exists for near-real-time error rate, p95 latency, database health, and regional segmentation.
Canary cohorts can be isolated without systematically excluding traffic patterns needed to reveal the changed routing and database behavior.
One business day provides enough time for the proposed stages and observation windows.
risks: A nine-minute application rollback cannot by itself guarantee compliance once customer error rate exceeds 1%, making rapid detection and feature-flag mitigation critical.
Database read-pattern regressions may not be mitigated by the routing flag and could continue during application rollback.
Automatic thresholds may cause false aborts from normal regional or third-party latency variance.
A 1% canary may miss rare request types, low-volume regions, or load-dependent effects that appear only at larger stages.
Additive schema changes can still create operational problems if new writes, indexes, defaults, or query plans impose unexpected load, even when structural compatibility is preserved.
evidence_needed: Measured feature-flag propagation and confirmation that disabling routing restores the prior path without redeployment.
Exact monitoring latency, alert evaluation windows, and automated-abort execution time.
Baseline and acceptable regression thresholds for global and per-region error rate, p95 latency, database latency, connection saturation, and query load.
Rollback rehearsal showing the old version safely handles all data written by the new version and confirming the nine-minute rollback duration under production conditions.
Traffic-volume calculations showing that every rollout stage can achieve statistically useful signals and complete within one business day.
Analysis of which database read-pattern failures are detectable before customer error rate breaches the constraint.

citations.claim: The previous three routing regressions were detectable through error rate or p95 latency within four minutes.
The schema fields are additive and safely ignored by the old application version, supporting rollback without schema downgrade.
A 1% canary needs about 12 minutes to produce statistically useful latency signals.
A global application-version rollback takes nine minutes.
Production-identical staging would take six weeks and would still miss third-party latency variance.
Feature flags can disable the new routing path without redeployment, but database read-pattern changes require application rollback.
Customer error rate must not exceed 1% for more than five minutes.
Rollback must not require a schema downgrade.
A healthy rollout should reach all traffic within one business day.

artifact.recommendation: Use staged canaries with automatic abort thresholds, backward-compatible additive schema changes, and a preplanned two-layer rollback. Begin at 1% traffic for at least 12 minutes, then advance through progressively larger regional or traffic cohorts only while error rate and p95 latency remain healthy. Automatically disable the new routing path via feature flag at conservative thresholds below the customer limit; if database read-pattern metrics regress, immediately initiate application rollback. Complete the healthy rollout within one business day.
reasoning: A staged canary limits blast radius while exposing production-only behavior that staging cannot perfectly reproduce.
The 1% canary needs about 12 minutes to produce useful latency evidence, so each initial observation window must be at least that long.
Prior routing regressions appeared in error rate or p95 latency within four minutes, making automatic monitoring suitable for early detection.

The application rollback takes nine minutes, which is longer than the permitted five-minute breach window. Therefore, abort thresholds must trigger before the global error rate reaches 1%, and the routing feature flag should provide the fastest first response.
The additive schema is safely ignored by the old application, allowing application rollback without a schema downgrade.

Waiting six weeks for production-identical staging would miss the one-business-day rollout objective without eliminating third-party latency uncertainty, while a global-at-once deployment creates unacceptable blast radius.
considerations: Define separate automatic thresholds for canary error rate, global customer error rate, p95 latency, database latency, connection saturation, and read load.
Use conservative thresholds that account for the nine-minute rollback duration; do not wait for a sustained 1% global error rate before aborting.
Pause progression after each cohort long enough to cover both the historical four-minute detection interval and statistically adequate traffic volume.
Keep new-schema writes backward compatible throughout rollout and rollback, and defer any destructive schema cleanup until the old version is no longer needed.
Exercise both feature-flag disablement and application rollback before release, with named owners and automated commands.
A feasible same-day sequence could use 1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, and 100% stages, adjusted by regional traffic volume and risk.
assumptions: Traffic allocation can be controlled by percentage and preferably by region or cohort.
Feature-flag propagation is substantially faster than the nine-minute application rollback.
Automatic monitoring and abort actions can operate continuously across all regions.
The old application remains deployable and compatible with all data written during the new release.
The one-business-day requirement applies only when all health gates pass.
risks: A 1% canary may miss region-specific, low-frequency, or scale-dependent failures that emerge only at larger stages.
Database read-pattern regressions cannot be fully mitigated by disabling the routing feature and may persist during the nine-minute rollback.
No stated feature-flag propagation time proves that routing errors can be contained within five minutes.
Automatic thresholds that are too sensitive may cause false aborts; thresholds that are too permissive may violate the customer error budget.
Global aggregate metrics can hide severe impact within a small region or customer cohort.
Progressing too quickly after the initial canary could expose traffic before delayed database effects become visible.
evidence_needed: Measured feature-flag propagation and confirmation times across every region.
Baseline and release-specific thresholds for error rate, p95 latency, database latency, connection utilization, and read amplification.
Expected global error-rate contribution at each rollout stage under plausible canary failure rates.
Rollback drill results confirming the nine-minute duration and old-version compatibility with newly written data.
Traffic-volume calculations establishing statistically useful observation windows for later stages and low-volume regions.
Evidence about delayed or cumulative database effects to determine whether observation windows longer than 12 minutes are required.

citations.claim: The previous three routing regressions were detectable through error rate or p95 latency within four minutes.
The schema additions are backward compatible because the old application safely ignores the new fields.
A 1% canary needs about 12 minutes to yield statistically useful latency signals.
A global application rollback takes nine minutes.
Production-identical staging would take six weeks and still would not reproduce third-party latency variance.
The routing path can be disabled without redeployment, but database read-pattern changes require application rollback.

strengths: Selects the clearly best-supported option: staged canaries with automatic aborts and backward-compatible schema changes.
Correctly distinguishes fast routing mitigation via feature flag from application rollback required for database read-pattern failures.
Uses the evidence appropriately: a 12-minute minimum 1% canary window, four-minute historical detection, nine-minute rollback, additive schema compatibility, and staging limitations.
Recognizes that a nine-minute rollback alone cannot guarantee the five-minute error-rate constraint.
Addresses regional masking, rare traffic, scale-dependent failures, false aborts, rollback rehearsal, ownership, and post-rollout monitoring.
Clearly separates supported conclusions, assumptions, risks, and evidence still needed.
weaknesses: The suggested 1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, 100% progression is plausible but not justified by quantitative blast-radius or timing analysis.
The report does not provide an explicit same-day schedule proving that all observation windows, decisions, and rollback readiness fit within one business day.
Abort-policy language remains qualitative; no concrete threshold, measurement window, monitoring delay, or action deadline is specified.
It does not clearly define whether the 1% canary is global, regional, or representative across regions and request classes.
The reports are highly duplicative, and the visible artifacts do not identify which single research report is the intended review target.
unsupported: The claim that automatic monitoring is suitable for early detection generalizes from only three prior routing regressions and does not establish coverage for database, regional, cumulative, or novel failures.
The assumption that feature-flag disablement can satisfy the five-minute constraint is unsupported because propagation, detection, evaluation, and recovery times are not provided.
The proposed rollout stages are unsupported by traffic-volume, statistical-power, regional-distribution, or load-scaling calculations.
The assertion that the healthy rollout can complete within one business day is not demonstrated with a timeline.
Structural schema compatibility does not by itself prove semantic compatibility with every value or record written by the new application.
missing: A precise control objective specifying whether the 1% limit is global, per region, per customer cohort, or measured by another scope.
An end-to-end mitigation-time budget covering telemetry delay, threshold evaluation, automation dispatch, feature-flag propagation, recovery confirmation, and application rollback.
A quantitative mapping from canary failure rates at each stage to global customer error rate and maximum exposure duration.
Explicit database-specific abort signals and thresholds that can trigger early enough despite the nine-minute rollback.
A rollout timetable, including observation periods and decision overhead, demonstrating completion within one business day.
Validation that canary allocation represents affected regions, request types, tenants, database shards, and third-party paths.
A policy for delayed regressions, including longer soak periods or post-100% automatic rollback criteria.
Contingency handling if the feature flag fails, rollback stalls, or both routing and database regressions occur together.
incorrect_assumptions: Treating a 12-minute statistically useful latency window as necessarily sufficient for database or delayed effects is unwarranted; the evidence only establishes useful latency signals at 1% volume.
Assuming additive fields guarantee safe rollback overlooks semantic changes, new writes, indexes, defaults, query plans, and data-shape constraints, although the report partially acknowledges this.
Assuming thresholding below 1% is enough ignores the relationship among canary size, failure severity, telemetry delay, mitigation time, and metric scope.
Assuming one business day is sufficient is premature without defining its duration across time zones and calculating the complete rollout schedule.
critical_risks: Database read-pattern failures may breach the five-minute customer-error constraint because their only stated mitigation takes nine minutes.
An unmeasured or unreliable feature-flag propagation path could invalidate the primary rapid-response mechanism for routing failures.
Aggregate global metrics could remain below 1% while a region or customer cohort suffers severe sustained errors.
Scale-dependent or cumulative database effects may appear only after larger stages or after reaching 100%, when blast radius is substantial.
Automation based on poorly calibrated thresholds could either abort healthy releases repeatedly or react too late to prevent a constraint violation.
recommended_changes: Specify exact automatic gates for global and per-region error rate, p95 latency, database latency, saturation, and read amplification, including rolling windows and recovery criteria.
Build a worst-case timing budget and require measured feature-flag mitigation to complete within the remaining portion of the five-minute limit after detection and evaluation latency.
Quantify expected global and cohort-level impact for a fully failing canary at every proposed stage, then derive stage sizes from the error constraint.
Provide a concrete same-day rollout schedule and define longer soak requirements for database and delayed effects.
Stratify or duplicate canaries across representative regions, request classes, tenants, and database shards instead of relying on an undifferentiated 1% sample.
Rehearse feature-flag disablement and rollback under production-like load, verifying old-version compatibility with all new writes and recording end-to-end recovery time.
Add explicit fail-safe procedures for flag failure, rollback failure, telemetry loss, and simultaneous routing/database regressions.
Clarify which of the two visible research artifacts is the single target; if both are intended, consolidate them and remove duplicated claims.

strengths: Selects staged canaries, the option best aligned with limited blast radius, production-only validation, and same-day completion.
Correctly connects the 12-minute 1% canary window, four-minute historical detection time, nine-minute application rollback, and five-minute error-duration constraint.
Uses the additive, backward-compatible schema evidence to support rollback without schema downgrade.
Distinguishes rapid routing-path deactivation from application rollback required for database read-pattern regressions.
Calls for regional as well as global telemetry, rollback rehearsal, accountable operators, manual stop authority, and continued post-rollout monitoring.
Clearly identifies why global-at-once deployment and waiting for production-identical staging are inferior under the stated evidence.
weaknesses: The proposed 1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, and 100% progression is illustrative rather than derived from failure impact, traffic volume, regional topology, or statistical power.
The policy does not specify exact health gates, evaluation windows, recovery criteria, minimum stable periods, or rules for resuming after an abort.
It does not present a concrete schedule proving that all stages, rollback drills, decision time, and observation windows fit within one business day.
The automatic rollback language is operationally ambiguous: database regressions require reliable detection and classification before the correct rollback action can be selected.
The analysis emphasizes p95 latency and error rate but does not adequately cover tail latency, timeouts, correctness failures, or database saturation that may precede customer errors.
unsupported: Feature-flag propagation is assumed to be fast and reliable enough to satisfy the five-minute constraint; no propagation or confirmation time is provided.
The claim that automatic aborts leave adequate margin against the five-minute constraint is not established without monitoring delay, threshold-window length, decision latency, and mitigation time.
The suggested stage sequence is unsupported by quantitative exposure or statistical analysis.
Compatibility with additive fields does not by itself prove that all new writes, defaults, indexes, query plans, or semantic changes are safe for the old application.
The conclusion that automatic monitoring is suitable rests on only three historical routing regressions and does not establish coverage for database, regional, delayed, or novel failure modes.
missing: A precise breach definition, including whether the 1% limit is global, per region, per customer cohort, or measured over a specific rolling window.
A timing budget from fault onset through telemetry ingestion, alert evaluation, abort execution, flag propagation or rollback, and verified recovery.
Quantitative abort thresholds for error rate, latency, database health, and canary-versus-control deltas.
A maximum safe exposure calculation for each stage under plausible canary failure rates.
Control-group comparison, statistical decision rules, and treatment of low-volume regions or rare request classes.
Explicit handling for partial feature-flag propagation, failed rollback, rollback-induced overload, and simultaneous regional incidents.
Database-specific safeguards such as read amplification, connection-pool pressure, replica lag, lock contention, query-plan changes, and data correctness checks.
Criteria for halting the rollout for the day versus retrying after investigation.
An explicit deployment order across regions and protection against correlated global dependencies.
incorrect_assumptions: It implicitly treats detection within four minutes as leaving time to mitigate within a five-minute breach window, although detection time alone nearly consumes that window and the breach may begin before detection.
It assumes the old version remains safely deployable based only on ignoring additive fields; semantic compatibility with data written by the new version is not fully established.
It assumes percentage canaries adequately represent global traffic despite acknowledged regional, rare-request, and scale-dependent risks.
It assumes one business day is sufficient without defining its duration, rollout start time, regional operating coverage, or required observation periods.

It may conflate the requirement to avoid more than five minutes above 1% error with a need to abort before reaching 1%; conservative triggering is prudent, but the exact necessary threshold depends on exposure and mitigation timing.
critical_risks: A database read-pattern regression could push customer errors above 1% for longer than five minutes because application rollback alone takes nine minutes.
Unknown feature-flag propagation and verification latency means the proposed primary mitigation may not meet the hard customer-impact constraint.
Global aggregate health gates could permit severe regional or cohort-specific harm while overall error rate remains below 1%.
Delayed, cumulative, or load-dependent database failures may pass early 12-minute canaries and emerge at larger stages.
Automation could select the wrong mitigation, fail partially, or oscillate if routing and database symptoms overlap.
recommended_changes: Define a formal rollout state machine with exact entry, promotion, pause, abort, recovery, and retry conditions.

Measure and budget every component of mitigation latency; require the total worst-case response time to fit the five-minute constraint or reduce canary exposure enough that a failed cohort cannot breach the global limit.
Derive stage sizes from maximum tolerable impact, regional representation, and statistical power instead of adopting an unvalidated fixed sequence.
Add per-region and per-cohort gates, canary-versus-control comparisons, tail-latency and timeout metrics, and database saturation and correctness indicators.
Require pre-release drills for feature-flag disablement, application rollback, rollback failure, and compatibility with all data written by the new version.
Specify database emergency controls beyond full rollback where feasible, such as read-path flags, query throttling, load shedding, or connection limits.
Provide a same-day timeline demonstrating that observation windows and decision overhead satisfy the rollout deadline.
Lower confidence until feature-flag timing, rollback rehearsal, monitoring latency, delayed database behavior, and stage-level traffic calculations are verified.

attacks: The recommendation does not actually demonstrate compliance with the hardest constraint. Database read-pattern failures require a nine-minute rollback, so any such failure that raises customer errors above 1% may violate the five-minute limit before recovery.
The rapid-response strategy depends on feature-flag propagation being fast, reliable, globally consistent, and capable of restoring health, but none of those properties is evidenced.

Detection within four minutes is being mistaken for mitigation within five minutes. Telemetry lag, evaluation windows, automation dispatch, propagation, and recovery verification could easily exhaust the remaining minute.
Evidence from only three routing regressions is too narrow to justify confidence in detecting novel routing faults, database saturation, correctness defects, regional failures, or delayed effects.
The fixed 1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, 100% sequence is arbitrary. It is not derived from maximum tolerable impact, statistical power, regional topology, or rollback duration.
A statistically useful latency signal after 12 minutes does not establish that 12 minutes is a sufficient soak period for cumulative, load-dependent, or database failures.
An undifferentiated percentage canary may systematically miss low-volume regions, rare request classes, large tenants, particular shards, and third-party paths affected by the change.
Additive fields prove structural tolerance only. They do not prove that the old version safely interprets values, defaults, indexes, query-plan changes, or records written by the new version.
Global aggregate gates could remain healthy while a small region or customer cohort experiences sustained catastrophic errors.
The recommendation promises completion within one business day without defining the day, deployment order, decision overhead, soak periods, or a schedule demonstrating feasibility.
The two-layer response assumes failures can be classified quickly as routing-related or database-related. Overlapping symptoms could trigger the wrong action or delay both actions.
The policy lacks a safe answer for telemetry loss, partial flag propagation, rollback failure, rollback-induced overload, or simultaneous routing and database regressions.
falsifiers: An end-to-end drill shows that fault onset to verified feature-flag recovery can exceed five minutes in any production region.
A production-like database regression drives customer errors above 1% and cannot be contained below that level during the nine-minute application rollback.
The old application fails, misreads data, or causes harmful queries when run against every record shape and database object produced by the new release.
Traffic analysis shows that the 1% cohort lacks representative coverage or sufficient samples for any affected region, request class, tenant, shard, or dependency.
Load testing shows a regression that appears only above an intended promotion stage or after a soak longer than 12 minutes.
Stage-level impact modeling shows that a fully failing canary can push the applicable customer error metric above 1% for longer than five minutes.
A concrete rollout timetable cannot accommodate statistically adequate observation windows, promotion overhead, and regional execution within one business day.
Historical incident replay shows that the proposed metrics or thresholds would miss, detect too late, or misclassify a material routing or database failure.
Feature-flag disablement does not fully restore the prior routing behavior, propagates inconsistently, or increases database load.
The customer constraint is interpreted per region or cohort rather than globally, invalidating stage sizes and aggregate abort gates based on global dilution.
evidence_gaps: Exact scope and computation of the 1% error constraint: global, regional, tenant-level, cohort-level, and the applicable rolling window.
Measured worst-case telemetry ingestion, threshold evaluation, automation dispatch, feature-flag propagation, rollback, and recovery-confirmation times by region.

Quantitative automatic thresholds and recovery criteria for errors, timeouts, tail latency, canary-control deltas, database latency, read amplification, saturation, replica lag, locks, and correctness.
Maximum customer impact at every stage under partial and total canary failure, including the nine-minute rollback interval.
Feature-flag reliability, regional consistency, confirmation mechanism, and proof that disabling the route restores health.
Rollback rehearsal under production-like load, including compatibility with all new writes and the possibility of rollback-induced overload.
Representative-cohort design covering regions, request types, tenants, database shards, third-party paths, and low-frequency operations.
Evidence about delayed, cumulative, and scale-dependent database behavior needed to choose defensible soak periods.
A formal rollout state machine defining promotion, pause, abort, rollback, recovery, retry, and stop-for-the-day conditions.
A concrete same-day schedule with regional order, observation windows, operational overhead, staffing coverage, and post-100% monitoring.
Fail-safe procedures and tested outcomes for telemetry loss, partial flag execution, failed rollback, and concurrent fault modes.
Whether additional database emergency controls—read-path flags, throttling, load shedding, or connection limits—can bridge the nine-minute rollback gap.

accepted_criticisms: The proposed policy does not demonstrate compliance with the five-minute error constraint for database read-pattern failures because the only stated application rollback takes nine minutes.

Feature-flag propagation, consistency, reliability, recovery effect, and end-to-end confirmation time are unmeasured, so routing-path disablement cannot yet be treated as a proven five-minute mitigation.
Four-minute historical detection is not equivalent to recovery within five minutes; telemetry, evaluation, dispatch, propagation, and verification consume additional time.
Three historical routing regressions provide insufficient evidence for novel, database, regional, correctness, cumulative, or load-dependent failures.
The illustrative 1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, 100% sequence is not quantitatively derived from tolerable impact, cohort coverage, statistical power, topology, or mitigation duration.
A useful latency signal after 12 minutes does not establish that a 12-minute soak detects delayed or scale-dependent database failures.
An undifferentiated percentage canary may omit low-volume regions, rare requests, large tenants, shards, and third-party paths.
Global aggregate gates can conceal severe regional or cohort-level failures.
Completion within one business day has not been demonstrated with a concrete schedule, observation periods, deployment order, and decision overhead.
Routing and database symptoms may overlap, delaying or misdirecting automated mitigation.
The policy lacks defined responses for telemetry loss, partial flag propagation, rollback failure, rollback-induced overload, and concurrent fault modes.

Structural compatibility with additive fields does not alone prove safe rollback across new values, writes, indexes, defaults, query plans, and operational load; those require rehearsal and validation.
rejected_criticisms: The criticism that the report categorically treated 12 minutes as sufficient is overstated: it specified at least 12 minutes, recommended longer holds for sparse or variable traffic, and explicitly identified delayed database effects as a risk.
The criticism that the stage sequence was presented as mandatory is overstated: it was labeled suggested or feasible and expressly conditioned on traffic-volume validation and scheduling.

The claim that additive fields provide no relevant rollback evidence is too broad: the supplied evidence explicitly says the old application safely ignores them, which supports the no-schema-downgrade requirement, though it does not prove complete semantic and operational compatibility.

The report did not wholly overlook regional masking, rare traffic, scale effects, schema operational risks, or post-100% failures; it identified each as a risk or evidence gap. The valid criticism is that the controls were not made quantitative or mandatory.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Choose staged canaries with automatic aborts and backward-compatible schema changes, but do not authorize the proposed fixed progression yet. Before rollout, define the scope and window of the 1% constraint; derive representative cohort sizes and stage limits from worst-case impact; measure end-to-end telemetry and feature-flag recovery time by region; rehearse rollback and old-version compatibility with all new writes; add database emergency controls capable of bridging the nine-minute rollback; define per-region, per-cohort, tail-latency, correctness, and database gates; add failure contingencies and a formal rollout state machine; and prove a same-day schedule. If these checks cannot show that every credible failure remains below the permitted duration, hold the release rather than relying on the nine-minute rollback.
reasons: Staged canaries remain better supported than global-at-once deployment because they reduce initial blast radius while testing production-only behavior.
Waiting six weeks for production-identical staging remains unattractive because it would still omit third-party latency variance.
The original option selection was correct on the visible evidence, but the concrete rollout policy was too confident and insufficiently proven against the hardest constraint.
The nine-minute database rollback creates a direct compliance gap unless stage exposure alone prevents a global breach or faster database containment exists.
The evidence supports structural schema rollback compatibility, but broader semantic and operational compatibility remains unverified.
Accordingly, the recommendation changes from proceed with an illustrative staged sequence to conditionally approve staged canaries only after quantitative safety gates and drills are satisfied.

accepted_criticisms: The nine-minute application rollback cannot guarantee the five-minute customer-error constraint for database read-pattern failures; additional containment or stage-level impact limits are required.
Feature-flag propagation, reliability, regional consistency, and end-to-end recovery time are unverified.
Four-minute historical detection does not establish mitigation within five minutes and covers only three routing regressions.
The proposed 1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, 100% stages are illustrative and lack quantitative derivation.
A 12-minute latency-signal window does not prove adequate soak time for delayed, cumulative, or scale-dependent failures.
An undifferentiated percentage canary and global aggregate gates can miss severe regional, tenant, request-class, shard, or dependency-specific failures.
The report does not demonstrate same-business-day feasibility with a concrete schedule.
Exact thresholds, metric scope, timing budgets, recovery criteria, rollout state transitions, and failure contingencies are missing.
Routing and database symptoms may overlap, delaying or misdirecting mitigation.
Safe rollback requires production-like validation of new writes and database effects beyond the stated field-level compatibility.
Confidence was too high given the unresolved hard-constraint risks.
rejected_criticisms: The criticism that additive fields establish only structural tolerance is too absolute: evidence explicitly states that the old application safely ignores those fields. However, it does not establish safety for every associated write, index, default, query plan, or load effect.

The staged-canary option itself is not invalidated. It remains better supported than global deployment or a six-week wait for an imperfect staging environment; the deficiencies concern readiness evidence and policy specification.
The report did not claim that 12 minutes detects every delayed database failure; it explicitly identified delayed and scale-dependent effects as risks and recommended longer holds where warranted.

The report did not unconditionally prove or promise same-day completion; it treated feasibility as an assumption and required a precomputed schedule, though the recommendation should have made this prerequisite stronger.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Choose staged canaries with automatic aborts and backward-compatible schema changes, but make release authorization conditional. Before rollout, define the 1% metric scope and window; measure worst-case detection-to-verified-mitigation time by region; drill feature-flag disablement and application rollback; prove old-version compatibility with all new writes and database effects; derive representative cohorts, stage sizes, and soak periods from impact and statistical analysis; add database emergency containment capable of bridging the nine-minute rollback; define per-region and per-cohort gates plus fail-safe procedures; and produce a feasible same-day schedule. If a database failure can exceed 1% errors for over five minutes despite these controls, do not release until exposure is reduced or faster containment exists. If all gates pass, proceed through quantitatively derived stages and continue automated monitoring after 100%.
reasons: Staged canaries still minimize initial blast radius while testing production-only behavior.
Global-at-once deployment is less defensible, and waiting six weeks for non-identical staging does not remove third-party variance.
The additive-schema evidence supports rollback without schema downgrade at the field level.
The visible evidence does not establish compliance with the hardest customer-impact constraint for database regressions.
Unknown feature-flag and telemetry timing prevents assurance that routing failures can be contained within five minutes.
The proper correction is to make rollout conditional and quantitatively derived, not to switch to either inferior option.

artifact.decision: Conditionally select staged canaries with automatic aborts and backward-compatible schema changes, but do not authorize rollout until the hard five-minute customer-error constraint is quantitatively demonstrated for routing and database failures.
artifact.action: Require measured end-to-end mitigation drills, stage-level impact modeling, representative cohorts, database emergency containment, exact regional/cohort gates, rollback compatibility validation, failure contingencies, and a feasible same-day schedule. Release only if these controls show that credible failures cannot keep the applicable customer error rate above 1% for more than five minutes; otherwise hold the release.
reasons: Staged canaries minimize initial blast radius while exercising production behavior that cannot be perfectly simulated.
Global deployment creates unnecessary exposure, while waiting six weeks for still-imperfect staging does not eliminate third-party latency variance.
The nine-minute application rollback cannot by itself satisfy the five-minute limit if a database regression drives the applicable error rate above 1%.
Historical detection within four minutes does not establish recovery within five minutes, especially when telemetry, evaluation, dispatch, propagation, and verification are unmeasured.
Feature-flag disablement is a plausible routing safeguard, but its propagation time, consistency, reliability, and health-restoration effect are unverified.
The visible evidence supports field-level rollback compatibility without schema downgrade, but not complete semantic and operational compatibility with all new writes and database effects.
No fixed stage sequence, soak duration, or one-business-day timetable is justified by the supplied evidence.
evidence: Problem e1 states that three previous routing regressions were detectable through error rate or p95 latency within four minutes.
Problem e2 states that the new fields are additive and safely ignored by the old application.
Problem e3 states that a 1% canary yields statistically useful latency signals in about 12 minutes.
Problem e4 states that global application rollback takes nine minutes.
Problem e5 states that production-identical staging would take six weeks and still omit third-party latency variance.
Problem e6 states that a feature flag can disable new routing without redeployment, while database read-pattern changes require application rollback.
The stated constraints require no error rate above 1% for more than five minutes, no schema downgrade during rollback, and completion within one business day when healthy.
Both rebuttals independently converge on conditional staged rollout and identify the unresolved database-containment gap.
rejected_alternatives: Reject global-at-once deployment because it maximizes blast radius and offers no compensating evidence that the five-minute constraint can be protected.

Reject an unconditional six-week staging hold because the proposed environment would still fail to reproduce third-party latency variance; holding remains appropriate only until the staged rollout's safety prerequisites are satisfied.
Reject immediate use of the illustrative 1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, 100% progression because it is not derived from impact limits, topology, representativeness, statistical power, or mitigation duration.
Reject reliance on the routing feature flag as the sole rapid-response mechanism because it does not contain database read-pattern regressions and has no measured recovery timing.
Reject treating a 12-minute latency window as a generally sufficient soak period because delayed, cumulative, correctness, and scale-dependent failures remain untested.
minority: A stricter interpretation could choose the hold option immediately because current evidence does not prove compliance with the hardest constraint. The preferred decision instead conditionally selects the staged-canary architecture while withholding release authorization.

A permissive interpretation could proceed with very small canaries on the theory that global error dilution prevents a breach, but the constraint's scope and cohort-level impact are undefined, so that interpretation is unsafe.
unresolved: Whether the 1% limit is global, regional, tenant-level, cohort-level, or evaluated over a particular rolling window.
Worst-case telemetry, evaluation, automation, feature-flag propagation, rollback, and recovery-verification times by region.
Whether disabling routing consistently restores health and whether partial propagation can be detected.
